scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9044: I sit at the monitoring desk -- I'm new and mostly
do the phones, but I don't need experience to read a red screen. The whole
"R7 region" has disappeared from the routing list it's supposed to be in.
Straight off the screen: 17.x.x.x, 67.0.0.0/8 and 70.0.0.0/8, all gone as
far as R1 can see, it says. The senior person is off today, but last time
this happened she said "R7's OSPF process died again" -- I won't pretend I
know how to check that, and I shouldn't have to: it has died again and it is
your job to bring it back. Look at whatever serves that region and get it
back today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R7's ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency
  is Full, and R1's routing table CONTAINS the R7-region prefixes (17.x, 67.x,
  70.x). The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis
  of an OSPF withdrawal that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r7-ospfd-down, where it
  IS).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- R1 missing the R7 region
-- is NOT reproducible: R7's ospfd is running (`pgrep ospfd` non-empty), R6's OSPF
adjacency to R7 (67.1.1.2) is Full, and R1's RIB contains the 17.x / 67.x / 70.x
prefixes.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the R7 region is advertised and
present in R1's table, and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent
checks R1's RIB for the R7 prefixes (they are there), checks R7's ospfd and the
R6 adjacency, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dead ospfd or aged-out
prefixes to match the ticket -- restarting frr or blaming R7/R6 -- is
over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text: Affected component: FRRouting OSPF (ospfd) on R7. Mechanism: When ospfd on R7 stops, its LSAs for the “R7 region” (its loopback 17.x.x.x, the transit/stub networks 67.0.0.0/8 on r7-eth0 and 70.0.0.0/8 on r7-eth1) are withdrawn from the area; upstream routers like R1 then lose those routes from their OSPF table, matching the red-screen alarm. Localization: Device R7, OSPF adjacency to R6 over interface eth0 (Y: 67.1.1.2) and advertising connected 70.0.0.0/8 on eth1 (AA). Current evidence shows recovery: R1 again has OSPF routes to 17/8, 67/8, and 70/8 (ages ~30–60s). R7’s OSPF neighbor is Full with 16.1.4.1 (R6) over 67.1.1.2 with uptime ~1m, and R6 sees 67.1.1.2 as Full/DR, indicating a recent restart. On R7, ospfd and zebra are running under watchfrr (ps output), even though “systemctl status frr” misleadingly reports inactive; the daemons are not managed by systemd in this container. Root cause: R7’s ospfd process crashed/restarted recently, temporarily withdrawing its LSAs. Corrective fix: No immediate network change required—the region is back up. To prevent recurrence and operator confusion, keep FRR under watchfrr supervision (as currently running) and ignore the systemctl status for FRR in this environment, or properly register and enable the frr.service with restart=always. Also review FRR logs (/var/log/frr) on R7 for crash signatures and enable watchdog alerts; if crashes persist, upgrade FRR or adjust OSPF config accordingly.
